title: Subsets and Combination Sum
excerpt: The gentlest problem in the section, done slowly. One parameter separates 2 to the n work from n factorial work, and combination sum is where pruning first earns its keep.
seoTitle: Combination Sum and Subsets: Backtracking with Pruning
seoDescription: Subsets and combination sum with backtracking: why the answer count is exponential, what the start index actually prevents, a full pruned trace, and why sorting the candidates sharpens the prune.

content.text: Subsets is the gentlest problem in this section, and it is worth doing carefully rather than quickly, since nothing here gets rejected, so you can watch the recursion's shape without a prune complicating the picture.
The task: given a list of distinct numbers, produce every subset, which for [1,2,3] is eight answers, from the empty set up to the whole thing.

body.text: Knowing the answer's size before you start

content.text: It pays to know how many answers to expect, because it tells you what your program is allowed to cost. Every item faces one independent decision, in or out, so with n items that is 2 multiplied by itself n times: 2 to the power of n subsets. For 3 items that is 8. For 20 items, about a million. For 40, over a trillion.

So there is no fast algorithm hiding here. Any correct program has to produce 2 to the power of
n

answers, and printing them alone takes that long. When the output is exponential the algorithm has to be too, and this is one of the rare cases where an exponential runtime is not a sign of a mistake.
The template from the introduction needs three things filled in: what a complete answer looks like, what choices exist at each step, and which of them are allowed.

The natural reading is that a state is a partial subset and a choice is "which item do I add next". Every state is already a valid subset, so every node in the tree records an answer rather than only the leaves. That is unusual and worth noticing: in most problems only complete states count.
Now a real problem appears. If each step may choose any item, you will build the same subset repeatedly under different orderings.

body.code:
Without a start index, choosing from all of [1,2,3] every time:

  [] -> [1] -> [1,2]        and        [] -> [2] -> [2,1]

Same set, built twice, and the tree keeps doing it. With start,
a branch only ever looks at items to the RIGHT of what it took.

content.text: The fix is a single parameter. Pass down a start index, and only ever choose items at or after it, so having taken item 2, later steps consider only items 3 onward. Each subset is then built in exactly one order and appears exactly once.
This one parameter is the difference between 2 to the power of
n
work and
n
factorial work. It is the most important line in the problem and it looks like nothing.
Step through and match the tree against the trace from the introduction. Every node is an answer here, so the count of recorded answers climbs steadily rather than only at the bottom.

body.text: Combination sum, where pruning finally appears

content.text: Subsets had no rules to break, so nothing was ever rejected, but combination sum adds one, and it is where the prune from the introduction earns its keep.
The task: given candidate numbers and a target, find every combination that sums to exactly the target, where each candidate may be used as many times as you like.
Two things change from subsets. First, since reuse is allowed, a recursive call passes
i
rather than

, so the same item stays available. Second, and this is the interesting part, you can tell a branch is doomed before finishing it. If the running total already exceeds the target, no amount of adding more positive numbers will bring it back down.

That single check cuts an entire subtree. Below is the tree for candidates 2, 3 and 5 with target 8, pruning on: step through it and watch every branch that gets cut the moment a partial sum overshoots.

Watch the branches-cut counter as you go. Each cut is a subtree a generate-and-filter approach would have explored all the way to the bottom before throwing it away. The deeper the tree, the more each cut saves.

Switch pruning off and back on. The candidates, the target and the answers all stay the same, so the only thing worth watching is the node counter. That difference is the entire value of thinking about the problem before writing the loop.

If the candidates are sorted, the prune gets stronger. When you meet a candidate larger than the remaining target, every candidate after it is larger too, so instead of skipping this one you can stop the loop entirely.
That turns a
continue
into a
break
and skips the rest of the row rather than one cell of it. The sort costs
n log n
once and pays for itself immediately. It is a good habit generally: sorting the input often makes a prune sharper.
Compare this against the subsets code from the introduction. The skeleton is untouched. What changed is the stopping test, one prune, and
i
in place of
Passing i + 1 when reuse is allowed, or i when it is not.
These two problems differ by that single character, and getting it wrong produces answers that look plausible. If your combination sum output is missing every repeated-element answer, this is why.
Dropping the start index in subsets.
You get every permutation of every subset, so the answer count jumps from 8 to 16 on three items and the duplicates are not obvious at a glance.
Checking the total only at the leaves is correct and slow, since the whole point is to reject as early as the rules allow.
Assuming the prune still holds with negative candidates.

If a candidate can be negative, exceeding the target no longer means the branch is dead, because a later negative can bring the sum back. The prune quietly becomes wrong. Check the constraints before relying on it.

questions.prompt: What is the start index in the subsets solution actually preventing?

options.label: The same subset being built in several different orders

questions.prompt: How many subsets does a list of 20 distinct items have?

options.label: About a million, since it is 2 to the power of 20

questions.prompt: In combination sum, why does the recursive call pass i rather than i + 1?

options.label: Because a candidate may be used more than once, so it stays available
To avoid skipping the last candidate

questions.prompt: A candidate exceeds the remaining target and the list is sorted. What is better than continue?

options.label: break, since every later candidate is larger and will also fail
return, since the whole search is finished
